utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning to the Registrar, first, I would like to be sure that the interpretation is going through and that everybody is hearing. Does everybody hear me? Prosecution? Registrar? Mr. Babic? The accused? Do you hear? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC [Original in Serbo-Croat]: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning to the Registrar, would you please call the case on our agenda this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-96-22-PT, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. For this hearing we have the initial appearance. Pursuant to Rule 62, I would like to ask, first of all, who is representing Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am Eric Ostberg; I appear this morning with my learned friend Mr. Mark Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: The Defence is represented by Jovan Babic, a solicitor from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. The accused, would you rise, please, and state your identity? Mr. Erdemovic, date of your birth, your nationality, the place of your birth and where you are currently residing or where you were currently residing before you were transferred to the Tribunal. THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: My name is Drazen Erdemovic. I was born in Tuzla in 1971. I am a Croat by nationality. Before coming to The Hague, I was an inhabitant of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated. This initial hearing is based on the rules and our statutes, specifically Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal, 21(B) devoted the rights of the accused and 62, having the rules of procedure and evidence, which provides that as soon as the accused has had the indictment confirmed by the confirming judge, the accused must be presented to a Trial Chamber which is composed of judges who did not confirm the indictment. First of all, I would like to turn to Mr. Babic: Mr. Babic, have you received a copy of the indictment in a language which you understand and which, of course, the accused understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have received the text of the indictment in Serbo-Croatian and both the accused and myself have understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please remain standing. I would like to ask you another question. Have you deliberated a long time about the contents of this indictment with the accused and explained what defence strategy can be used, which you are going to use with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: With my client, I spent some time, several hours, studying the indictment and studying his rights according to the Statute and Rules of the Tribunal. I think that he had enough time to comprehend what he is charged with by this indictment and to understand his rights on that basis.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. You may be seated. Mr. Erdemovic, would you please rise? You have heard what you your counsel has just said. On behalf of my colleagues and on behalf of the International Tribunal, I would like to ask you the same question, the one that I asked your attorney: Have you read the indictment, have you had the opportunity, have you had the time, to speak about it with Mr. Babic? Have the facts in that indictment been presented to you, have they been presented to you in a language which you understand, that is, Serbo-Croat? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: Yes, your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Were you reminded as well that before this international court you could be defended equitably and in public? Do you understand the scope of these terms? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: Your Honour, allow me to explain. Before the indictment was issued against me

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Erdemovic, for the moment, like everybody in this Tribunal, I am following rules which are the Rules of our Statute, the Rules of the International Tribunal. This is a procedure which is applied for all accused. You have been accused before this Tribunal. I would like to be sure about a certain number of conditions. It is self-evident the Tribunal will listen to any statement that you wish to make and you will have the opportunity to make them at the point when the Tribunal orders you to do so. For the moment you may be seated, Mr. Erdemovic. I would like now, pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, to ask the Registrar to read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor of the Trial Chamber against Drazen Erdemovic. Indictment. The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to his authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the Tribunal charges: Drazen Erdemovic with a Crime Against Humanity or, alternatively, a Violation of the Laws or Customs of War, as set forth below: On 16th April 1993, the Security Council of the United Nations, acting pursuant to Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, adopted resolution 819, in which it demanded that all parties to the conflict in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina treat Srebrenica and its surroundings as a safe area which should be free from any armed attack or any other hostile act. Resolution 819 was reaffirmed by resolution 824 on 6th May 1993 and by resolution 836 on 4th June 1993. On or about 6th July 1995, the Bosnian Serb army commenced an attack on the UN "safe area" of Srebrenica. This attack continued through until 11th July 1995, when the first units of the Bosnian Serb army entered Srebrenica. Thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians who remained in Srebrenica during this attack fled to the UN compound in Potocari and sought refuge in and around the compound. Between 11th and 13th July 1995, Bosnian Serb military personnel summarily executed an unknown number of Bosnian Muslims in Potocari and Srebrenica. Between 12th and 13th July 1995, the Bosnian Muslim men, women and children who had sought refuge in and around the UN compound in Potocari were placed on buses and trucks under the control of Bosnian Serb military personnel and police and transported out of the Srebrenica enclave. Before boarding these buses and trucks, Bosnian Muslim men were separated from Bosnian Muslim women and children and were transported to various collection centres around Srebrenica. A second group of approximately 15,000 Bosnian Muslim men, with some women and children, fled Srebrenica on 11th July 1995 through the woods in a large column in the direction of Tuzla. A large number of the Bosnian Muslim men who fled in this column were captured by or surrendered to Bosnian Serb army or police personnel. Thousands of Bosnian Muslim men who had been either separated from women and children in Potocari or who had been captured by or surrendered to Bosnian Serb military or police personnel were sent to different collection sites outside of Srebrenica including, but not limited to, a hangar in Bratunac, a soccer field in Nova Kasaba, a warehouse in Kravica, the primary school and gymnasium of "Veljko Lukic-Kurjak" in Grbavci, Zvornik municipality and diverse fields and meadows along the Bratunac-Milici road. Between 13th July 1995 and approximately 22nd July 1995, thousands of Bosnian Muslim men were summarily executed by members of the Bosnian Serb army and Bosnian Serb police at diverse locations including, but not limited to, a warehouse at Kravica, a meadow and a dam near Lazete and diverse other locations. On or about 16th July 1995, Drazen Erdemovic other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Bosnian Serb army were ordered to a collective farm near Pilica. The farm is located northwest of Zvornik in the Zvornik Municipality. On or about 16th July 1995, Drazen Erdemovic and other members of his unit were informed that bus loads of Bosnian Muslim civilian men from Srebrenica, who had surrendered to Bosnian Serb military or police personnel, would be arriving throughout the day at this collective farm. On or about 16th July 1995, buses containing Bosnian Muslim men arrived at the collective form in Pilica. Each bus was full of Bosnian Muslim men, ranging from approximately 17-60 years of age. After each bus arrived at the farm, the Bosnian Muslim men were removed in groups of about 10, escorted by members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment to a field adjacent to farm buildings and lined up in a row with their backs facing Drazen Erdemovic and members of his unit. On or about 16th July 1995, Drazen Erdemovic did shoot and kill and did participate with other members of his unit and soldiers from another brigade in the shooting and killing of unarmed Bosnian Muslim men at the Pilica collective farm. These summary executions resulted in the deaths of hundreds of Bosnian Muslim male civilians. The Accused. Drazen Erdemovic was born on 25th November 1971 in the municipality of Tuzla. He was a soldier in the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Bosnian Serb army. He is currently in custody in the UN detention facility in The Hague. General allegations. At all relevant times to this indictment, a state of armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Drazen Erdemovic is individually responsible for the crime alleged against him in this indictment pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Individual criminal responsibility includes committing, planning, instigating, ordering or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation or execution of any crimes referred to in Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal. Counts 1 and 2 (Crime Against Humanity) (Violation of the Laws or Customs of War). By his acts in relation to the events described in paragraph 12, Drazen Erdemovic committed: Count 1: A Crime Against Humanity punishable under Article 5(a) (murder) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Alternatively, count 2: A violation of the Laws or Customs of War punishable under Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal and recognised by Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions. Signed, Richard Goldstone, Prosecutor of this Tribunal, 22nd May 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Erdemovic, would you rise, please? According to what you said before, you understood what is contained in this indictment as well as the charges against you, those charges which the Prosecution has made against you. Have you spoken about these charges with your counsel, Mr. Babic? I am asking you a question now. THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you prepared to plead, given the fact that the Tribunal would like to recall to you that you can plead either guilty or not guilty? This is the procedure which was adopted in this Tribunal with it being understood, of course, that the consequences are not the same. I will explain them to you. If you plead not guilty, you are entitled to a trial during which, of course, with your lawyer you will contest the charges and the allegations and the charges presented against you by the Prosecutor, as I will remind you. Alternatively, either one or the other violations, crime against humanity or war crime, violation of laws or customs of war. If you plead guilty, the trial will continue but completely differently, which I am sure you understand but which I have to explain to you. At that point you will have the opportunity during another hearing at a date which we will set at that point in agreement with everybody, you will plead guilty but you will plead under other circumstances, that is, that there were attenuating circumstances, mitigating circumstances, or aggravating circumstances. Then there will be a discussion between your attorney and the Prosecution which will not be same. Having explained this to you, the Tribunal must now ask you whether you are prepared to plead and do you plead guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: Your Honour, I have told my counsel that I plead guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you plead guilty, I must also ask you another question. You heard that in the indictment which was drafted by the Office of the Prosecution against you, it provides for a charge which may be one or the other, that either a crime against humanity or a violation of the laws or customs of war. The text of our Statute obliges me to ask you whether you are pleading guilty on one of the charges, that is, there are acts, they were read to you, the Tribunal understands that you accept these facts and that they have been classified a certain way legally. This is part of international law. It is a bit difficult for you, but I will try to explain it to you in a more simple fashion, that is, there are acts and these are the acts which you have just recognised that, yes, you were at Srebrenica at such and such a moment. I think that the Prosecutor will make things very clear for us. The Prosecutor classifies them, which means that it determines a certain number of conditions from which a criminal violation has been charged. At the stage that we are now in these proceedings, which is at the beginning, the proceedings against you, Mr. Erdemovic, given the facts as they are today, that is, the fact that you have recognised what happened, that you were present, the various acts could either be classified as a crime against humanity or what we call violations of the laws or customs of war. Having said this, if there had been a trial, after the Tribunal would decide what, in fact, you were guilty of or not guilty of. In this case, since you have just said that you are pleading guilty, I must ask you if you are pleading guilty to the crime against humanity, that is, the version of the facts which for the Prosecutor would be a crime against humanity, or if it is a violation of the laws or customs of war. I suppose that you have spoken about this with your attorney? Mr. Erdemovic, could you answer us on that point which is an important one? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: I plead guilty for point one, crime against humanity.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated for now, Mr. Erdemovic. The Tribunal is now noting what you have said. It will have the opportunity to ask you later on about other questions to make sure that this has been an honest plea which has been entered. Now I am turning to the Office of the Prosecution, noting the fact that what has been said has just been recorded in the records of this hearing by the Registrar, therefore, Mr. Erdemovic is pleading guilty to the count, crime against humanity. I believe that we will most likely reject the other count, that is, violation of the laws or customs of war. But, before doing so, I would like to turn to the Office of the Prosecution and ask whether it would like to explain the acts, what are the facts of which Mr. Erdemovic is being accused and what you are accusing him of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, your Honour. We have just heard through the reading of the indictment by the Registrar the facts behind the indictment. I would just shortly summarise them and using the words I used when we the other day had the deferral hearing before another Trial Chamber: Drazen Erdemovic present here in the courtroom today was a soldier in the 10th Sabotage Detachment of what was then the Bosnian-Serb army. This unit and soldiers from another brigade of the same army were ordered to this collective farm, which we just heard of and by the name of Pilica. There he was ordered to go to receive bus loads of Muslim civilian men who had surrendered or had been apprehended fleeing from Srebrenica by military or police personnel. They were brought by these buses to this remote farm. The date was 16th July, 1995. The soldiers ordered to this farm were given the task to summarily execute those civilian men who were brought on the buses. These executions at the farm resulted, as we heard in the indictments, in the death of hundreds of Muslim men. Drazen Erdemovic was a member of this squad who had the task to execute the people and, indeed, he did do what he was tasked to do, and took part in the execution of these people which we have no exact figure of, but we are talking about hundreds of Muslim men. These, your Honours, are the facts behind the indictment now put into two different counts. From the point of view of the Prosecutor, of course, we accept the plea made today by Erdemovic. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostberg. Mr. Erdemovic, would you rise, please? You heard the version of the facts which the Prosecutor has just stated. Do you agree with what he said, that you were present on the premises, the way the buses arrived and then the facts which resulted in the deaths of this still undetermined number of civilians? Do you agree with what the Prosecution has just stated? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: I agree with everything that the Prosecutor has said and I have more to add. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 28 to 31.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you want to add something? You may do this before the Tribunal. You know that from this point on I will explain to you that there will be another hearing which will the hearing to determine the penalty which may be applied to you. What would you like to add, Mr. Erdemovic? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: Your Honour, I had to do this. If I had refused, I would have been killed together with the victims. When I refused, they told me: "If you are sorry for them, stand up, line up with them and we will kill you too". I am not sorry for myself but for my family my wife and son who then had nine months, and I could not refuse because then they would have killed me. That is all I wish to add.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Erdemovic. Try to get a hold of yourself. Sit down for a moment. I will ask you some other questions. Mr. Erdemovic, would you rise, please, again? The Tribunal must be sure that you know what you are doing because you know that pleading guilty or not guilty does not have the same consequences. You are before a Tribunal and the Tribunal must determine a penalty for your behaviour. At the proper time it will do so and, of course, we will hear all the parties. We will attempt to organise that hearing in order to see at the end of this one how we are going to organise the second one where you can explain yourself, but you cannot go back on the facts to which you have pleaded guilty. This is finished now and this is something that the Tribunal wants to be sure you really understand and that you your plea is sincere. You are represented by Mr. Babic. Are you satisfied with his representation, with your counsel? Have you been able to discuss things with your attorney under the most desirable conditions? THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: Your Honour, I am satisfied with the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. This is not the indictment now I am talking about. I want to know whether through the contacts that you have had, were you able to have counsel of your choice? If I ask you this question it is because the Tribunal had to appoint counsel that was not on the list of counsel which the Registrar maintains. You wish to have Mr. Babic and the Tribunal agreed to your request. Therefore, you spoke about everything you would use for your defence. Therefore, from this point on you have given up the right to a trial to determine whether or not you are guilty. This must be clear to you, clear between you and the Tribunal. At the same time, do you understand the penalties which will be imposed on you, if they are, which is something that the Tribunal will determine? Has Mr. Babic explained what these penalties consist of? I believe Mr. Babic did so, but I would like to remind you that the crimes that this Tribunal is charged with punishing can be punished by a sentence of life imprisonment. In this respect, I would like the Registrar to read the relevant Articles of the Statute and of the Rules dealing with the penalties. You may sit down now. This is a bit long, what has to be read. Turning to the Registrar, could you read so that the accused really understands all of our rules and procedures having to do with penalties, 24 of the Statute and 101 in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Article 24 of the Statute of the International Tribunal, Penalties, (1): "The penalty imposed by the Trial Chamber shall be limited to imprisonment. In determining the terms of imprisonment, the Trial Chambers shall have recourse to the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia". Paragraph 2: "In imposing the sentences, the Trial Chambers should take into account such factors as the gravity of the offence and the individual circumstances of the convicted person". Paragraph 3: "In addition to imprisonment, the Trial Chambers may order the return of any property and proceeds acquired by criminal conduct, including by means of duress to their rightful owners". Rule 101 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, (A): "(A) Any convicted person may be sentenced to life imprisonment for a term up to and including the remainder of his life; (B) In determining the sentence, the Trial Chamber shall take into account the factors mentioned in Article 24(2) of the Statute, as well as such factors as (i) any aggravating; (ii) any mitigating circumstance, including the substantial co-operation with the Prosecution by the convicted person before or after conviction; (iii) the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia; (iv) the extent to which any penalty imposed by a court of any state on the convicted person for the same act has already been served as referred to in Article 10(3) of the Statute. (C) The Trial Chamber shall indicate whether multiple sentences shall be served consecutively or concurrently; (D) the sentence shall be pronounced in public and in the presence of the convicted person, subject to sub-rule 102(B). (E) credit shall be given to the convicted person for the period, if any, during which the convicted person was detained in custody pending his surrender to the Tribunal or pending trial or appeal".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, would you rise again? On behalf of my colleagues and on behalf the Tribunal, I would like to ask you before you decided to plead guilty or not guilty whether you were threatened or promised anything in order to orientate you in one direction rather than another? Were you told, for example, you must plead guilty, or you have to do this, you must do that? This is a question I must ask you. THE ACCUSED ERDEMOVIC: No, no one threatened me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In these conditions then, I believe you can be seated again, Mr. Erdemovic. The Trial Chamber notes definitively the plea of guilty by Mr. Erdemovic and asks that it be placed on the record of this hearing. The Trial Chamber also decides that for the follow-up of this hearing to work only with count 1, and to reject and ask the Prosecution whether it has any objection in giving up the second count?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No, none, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you have any objection to giving up the second count since it was an alternative? MR. BABIC: No, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then we now have the following situation and I am saying this so that the accused understands fully what is being said. The accused Erdemovic has just pleaded guilty to count 1, crime against humanity. Therefore, at this point the Tribunal must determine the appropriate sentence. Of course, the trial is not in a position to pronounce this sentence since it does not have a great many elements that it needs, elements which no longer have to do with guilt but have to do with the personality of Erdemovic and also of the environment and the context of motivation which was present when the acts were committed as related by the Prosecution in the indictment. Mr. Registrar, would you now read us Rule 100 which will determine how we will set up the hearing, which will take us to the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Rule 100, pre-sentencing procedure: "If a Trial Chamber finds the accused guilty of a crime, the Prosecutor and the Defence may submit any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. I would now like to consult very briefly with my colleagues at the Bench. (The Judges conferred)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal has deliberated and has taken the decision, first, having to do with the organisation of the hearing which will lead to a sentence. The Tribunal has just decided that it will ask for a psychiatric evaluation of Mr. Erdemovic without prejudice, of course, to the requests which the Office of the Prosecutor might make or which the Defence might make. But, for the moment, it will be an evaluation which the Tribunal has ordered. Registrar, are you capable or in a position to have the accused examined by an authorised physician?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can have a psychiatric evaluation carried out quickly, if the Tribunal so wishes. I believe that a reasonable time period would be, say, three weeks.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal has now ordered a psychiatric evaluation that can be given to two practitioners, a psychiatrist and a psychologist. Registrar, would you note in the Minutes of this hearing that this request has been made and that it will appear in an order and ask the Registrar to draft this order as quickly as possible since Mr. Erdemovic must be examined, and for the organisation of the hearing which will lead to the sentence. During the hearing the Tribunal must have all information about everything that Mr. Erdemovic wants to say about the facts which led to his indictment, the circumstances surrounding it, the motivation particularly, and as well perhaps to call in witnesses the Prosecutor must be able to bring in any information which is relevant. I would first like to turn to the Defence and ask Mr. Babic whether he intends to request that the Tribunal do this or that or to call in any number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to make two requests and proposals, two motions. One will be incomplete because it pertains to a witness of whom my client said that on one occasion during certain operations, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: (redacted). This would be very important from the standpoint of the elucidation of the character of Mr. Erdemovic. Mr. Erdemovic only knows the witness's name (redacted) (redacted). That is my first motion. I take upon myself the obligation, but since our communication with Bosnia-Herzegovina is very difficult and it is highly problematic, whether the authorities of Bosnia will fulfil a request of this kind coming from me as the Defence of the accused, I would like to ask if the court could through the police authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina trace this witness and call him to a witness at this trial. Secondly, I fully agree with the decision of the court for psychological and psychiatric examination of Mr. Erdemovic. These will certainly be highly qualified experts from the Netherlands. I have absolutely no reservations regarding the quality of the findings of the experts from the Netherlands. However, we all know what happened in Yugoslavia. One of the consequences of all that has happened is that there are many young people who have suffered very grave psychological traumas and who simply cannot readjust to the society in which they live. In view of such a situation, psychologists and psychiatrists in Yugoslavia were faced with this challenge of studying the consequences in depth, not only theoretically but also in practice at various trials of individuals, so that a practice has developed, a certain amount of scientific knowledge has been gained, regarding the condition of such persons in Yugoslavia. So I think that it would be very useful for this court if the expert opinion could include two experts from Yugoslavia. They are court experts whom I would propose. They are university professors and together with the Dutch physicians they could jointly give an opinion on the condition and state of mind of Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning to the Prosecution, you have heard two requests from Mr. Babic. The Tribunal has decided to order a psychiatric evaluation. I am asking the question about whether in the request for the evaluation Mr. Babic, if necessary, when both parties are present have Mr. Erdemovic examined. I would like to know what your opinion is about this, and having to do specially with the first point, that is, hearing a witness (redacted) in a territory which, apparently, is difficult to gain access in order to find him. This would take a certain amount of time and we would like to move quickly in order to move to the hearing with the sentence. What is your opinion, please, about the two proposals of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that both proposals put forward to the court by Mr. Babic are reasonable and we would support each of those requests.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In so far as the Prosecution and the Defence agree, the evaluation of the Tribunal, I am now turning to the Registrar, could have added to the list, not 10 people perhaps, but I would like us to choose two experts that the Tribunal would designate, a psychiatrist and a psychologist, an expert which is chosen from a list which Mr. Babic might give to the Registrar. We have the idea of working that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I am afraid about the interference of competences between psychologists and psychiatrists because each have their own

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are all afraid of that, Mr. Babic! I do not think that we can today in such significant and important things. You understand that judges are not (indecipherable) before they pronounce sentences. They have to do the best they can. First, I think there is a list of experts in the Netherlands, in my country as well, in my colleagues' countries and in your country too. So we have to have some trust. Paragraphs the important point is knowing whether we can give you the satisfaction that you want, that is that you can draft a list quickly and indicate to the Registrar the name of an expert, whether it is a psychiatrist or a psychologist, who could be listed to the two experts whom the Trial Chamber will have appointed. The Tribunal wants to have those two experts, the psychiatrist and psychologist, and could you could add names to that. The Prosecutor has no objections to that. Then we will move that way. The second question is to do everything we can in order to locate this (redacted) (redacted). I do not know quite what should be done. Perhaps the Prosecutor knows what to do or the Registrar but, in any case, we must see one another. Do you have any witnesses that you want to call, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in the process at this time of formulating what witnesses we will present to the court. We are not in a position at the moment to advise the court, but we do intend to call some witnesses. We cannot identify them at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you have any other witnesses? Do you have witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal does have a concern. This is the first time that this is going to happen, the possible, I repeat possible, sentencing. You understand that the Tribunal must base itself on the penalties that were in effect in the former Yugoslavia. So perhaps this is something different to what we are used to, but the Tribunal would like to have information, a great part of which it already has. I would like to make things very clear between the Defence and the Prosecution, that as quickly as possible the Defence and the Prosecution should draft a short memo about what happened, specifically with the practices. The texts speak about the practices used in the former Yugoslavia. Now since this is not something which we know, there are penalties, there are codes and then there is the practice, the way these penalties were carried out, and since this cannot be given to one of the parties without affecting the other, I would suggest that each of the parties draft a short memorandum. The Tribunal, of course, since the Tribunal has been established, it has already done this kind of research, but it does has to be done now again in a more pragmatic manner. Before closing this hearing and setting the hearing for the sentences, I would like to first turn to the Prosecutor: Do you have a date for the hearing during which the witnesses would be heard, if you do call some, since you said you were going to call some? We have to schedule the number of days necessary. Have you already thought about a schedule? The Tribunal's calendar is already filling up and specifically the courtroom. Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour. We have been looking into this matter and we are prepared to have these hearings on 8th and 9th July this year.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 8th and 9th July. Today is 31st May. We have to have the report of the psychiatrist and psychologist, and also we will set a date for receiving their reports. We will receive the briefs and the memorandums having to do with the practices of the penalties. So, 8th and 9th July, would that be all right for Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have already agreed on this date with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Everybody agrees on 8th and 9th July. Since we are not really sure that we will have everything finished by 8th and 9th July, I would suggest that we have a status conference between the Prosecution and Mr. Babic on 24th June at 10.30. 24th June at 10.30. In the meantime, if possible before that, we must have received the report of the psychiatric evaluation. We will do research into trying to locate (redacted). We will organise the hearings of 8th and 9th July and see at that point whether we will be ready by 8th and 9th July. Are there any other questions? Turning to the Prosecution, have you any other comments you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Not for the moment, your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, have you any other comments you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Therefore, I now turn to my colleagues - this hearing is adjourned. (The hearing is adjourned) 5
